title: Song credits for arrangers
summary: He declined a song credit on Mr. Big Stuff, taking producer credit and half the royalties instead, and says arranging changes alone do not merit songwriting shares.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: On those songs, like Mr. Big Stuff, you said you made up changes and additions. Did you get a song credit on that?

Oh, no. They wanted to give it to me. I didn't want to accept that. You know, a lot of people in the business do that. But you can't blame, some things you can't, if I'm going to add something to a song, and it makes the song, you know, I don't see anything wrong in getting pieces of song, but it's just some unscrupulous people that might say one word in the tune and they want half of the song. Right. But, you know, like I said, man, Mr. Big Stuff, that was my, it was my company. I was the producer of it. I got half of the, I got the credit for it, I got half of the barrage because of the deal that we made with Malika, and I just figured, well, man, that's fine, you know. So I said, I'm getting my share.
There must have been other situations where you were just an arranger, and you went in and made changes on a song.

Yeah. But I mean, not enough to say that you should get part of the song. Yeah. You know, because that's your job, man, to do the best that you can with the song, and if there's any addition, if it's going to be beneficial to the song, then you should, you know, you should do it. But some people, man, they hear you writing a song, and they come up with, man, why don't put Joe Blow instead of Miss Blow, and they want half of the song.
